verified: Independent random key persists across database restart; private namespace is forbidden to public database APIs.
HTTP X-Api-Key and WebSocket identify api_key supply a real authorization identity.
Committed rotation invalidates old header credentials and cached WebSocket identities.
Persistence failures close authorization; damaged persisted keys are not silently regenerated.
Compiled configured service runs without TS loading or PATH programs.
Local users persist in private native_users namespace; asynchronous PBKDF2-SHA256 with 100000 iterations and Ed25519 JWTs.
HTTP Bearer, X-Access-Token, query access_token, WebSocket identify and login authenticate users; WebSocket user creation preserves caller identity.
Signed wrong issuer, audience, token type, username, fractional time and expired tokens reject; public request decoding can admit expired access tokens for refresh.
Logout and deletion revoke user keys and cached sessions; revocation survives restart; other users remain independent. Password changes preserve tokens as upstream does.
Subscription connection authorization requires matching usernames; notifications recheck authorization.
Compiled local user create/login/refresh/logout works without Python or TS loading.
limitations: Incomplete authorization: LDAP, trusted networks/proxies, one-shot tokens, authorization events, failed-login policy and configuration-file binding remain pending.
Native key storage uses a private namespace, not migration of the upstream authorized_users SQL table.
Requires an explicit component owner, endpoint registration and local provisioning; not yet the default Cycnumbris 500 machine adapter.
One active authorization owner per database is required; cross-process key cache coherence is not implemented.
Sequential local HTTP and CPU microbenchmarks do not prove concurrent print performance or target-board acceptance.
Native users have bounded input, 128-user capacity, 32 queued mutations and 1024 cached JWTs. These native limits differ from unrestricted upstream storage.
User creation requires a provisioned API key or authenticated user; no implicit trusted-network bootstrap. Issuer must be configured consistently across restarts.

WebSocket cached JWT sessions currently enforce access-token expiry on protected methods and notifications, requiring reauthentication; renewal and upstream long-lived session semantics remain to be closed.
Raw authorization headers and error text are not claimed to match all upstream edge cases. HTTP optional authentication accepts signed expired tokens, but rejects invalid signatures.
API-key microbenchmark rose from the prior 1.777 to 1.965 microseconds per request; both are within the 10 microsecond development budget, not proof of zero regression.

localUserBenchmark.scope: Desktop development regression only; no Python comparison or concurrent printing; hot cache 100000 decodes per round, 3 warmups and 5 retained rounds; cold 2000 distinct tokens; 20 sequential asynchronous password logins
